blocks.text: In a dentist’s operating room on a fine August morning in 1896. Not the usual tiny London den, but the best sitting room of a furnished lodging in a terrace on the sea front at a fashionable watering place. The operating chair, with a gas pump and cylinder beside it, is halfway between the centre of the room and one of the corners. If you look into the room through the window which lights it, you will see the fireplace in the middle of the wall opposite you, with the door beside it to your left; an M.R.C.S. diploma in a frame hung on the chimneypiece; an easy chair covered in black leather on the hearth; a neat stool and bench, with vice, tools, and a mortar and pestle in the corner to the right. Near this bench stands a slender machine like a whip provided with a stand, a pedal, and an exaggerated winch. Recognising this as a dental drill, you shudder and look away to your left, where you can see another window, underneath which stands a writing table, with a blotter and a diary on it, and a chair. Next the writing table, towards the door, is a leather covered sofa. The opposite wall, close on your right, is occupied mostly by a bookcase. The operating chair is under your nose, facing you, with the cabinet of instruments handy to it on your left. You observe that the professional furniture and apparatus are new, and that the wall paper, designed, with the taste of an undertaker, in festoons and urns, the carpet with its symmetrical plans of rich, cabbagy nosegays, the glass gasalier with lustres; the ornamental gilt rimmed blue candlesticks on the ends of the mantelshelf, also glass draped with lustres, and the ormolu clock under a glass cover in the middle between them, its uselessness emphasized by a cheap American clock disrespectfully placed beside it and now indicating 12 o’clock noon, all combine with the black marble which gives the fireplace the air of a miniature family vault, to suggest early Victorian commercial respectability, belief in money, Bible fetishism, fear of hell always at war with fear of poverty, instinctive horror of the passionate character of art, love and Roman Catholic religion, and all the first fruits of plutocracy in the early generations of the industrial revolution.

There is no shadow of this on the two persons who are occupying the room just now. One of them, a very pretty woman in miniature, her tiny figure dressed with the daintiest gaiety, is of a later generation, being hardly eighteen yet. This darling little creature clearly does not belong to the room, or even to the country; for her complexion, though very delicate, has been burnt biscuit color by some warmer sun than England’s; and yet there is, for a very subtle observer, a link between them. For she has a glass of water in her hand, and a rapidly clearing cloud of Spartan obstinacy on her tiny firm set mouth and quaintly squared eyebrows. If the least line of conscience could be traced between those eyebrows, an Evangelical might cherish some faint hope of finding her a sheep in wolf’s clothing﻿—for her frock is recklessly pretty﻿—but as the cloud vanishes it leaves her frontal sinus as smoothly free from conviction of sin as a kitten’s.

The Dentist, contemplating her with the self-satisfaction of a successful operator, is a young man of thirty or thereabouts. He does not give the impression of being much of a workman: his professional manner evidently strikes him as being a joke, and is underlain by a thoughtless pleasantry which betrays the young gentleman still unsettled and in search of amusing adventures, behind the newly set up dentist in search of patients. He is not without gravity of demeanor; but the strained nostrils stamp it as the gravity of the humorist. His eyes are clear, alert, of sceptically moderate size, and yet a little rash; his forehead is an excellent one, with plenty of room behind it; his nose and chin cavalierly handsome. On the whole, an attractive, noticeable beginner, of whose prospects a man of business might form a tolerably favorable estimate.
In spite of the biscuit complexion she has not the slightest foreign accent.
Putting it down on the ledge of his cabinet of instruments.
Every dentist has to begin on somebody.
Yes: somebody in a hospital, not people who pay.
Because you said it would be five shillings extra.

It amuses him to be treated in this fashion: he chuckles secretly as he proceeds to clean and replace his instruments. She shakes her dress into order; looks inquisitively about her; and goes to the window.
You don’t own the whole house, do you?
Taking the chair which stands at the writing-table and looking critically at it as she spins it round on one leg.
No: I have that on the hire-purchase system.
Looking about her again in search of further conclusions.
Six weeks. Is there anything else you would like to know?
The hint quite lost on her.
Of course not: anybody can see that. I meant sisters and mother and that sort of thing.
Hm! If you’ve been here six weeks, and mine was your first tooth, the practice can’t be very large, can it?
He shuts the cabinet, having tidied up everything.
It’s my system. I’m what’s called a five shilling dentist.

A handsome man in miniature, obviously the young lady’s twin, comes in eagerly. He wears a suit of terra-cotta cashmere, the elegantly cut frock coat lined in brown silk, and carries in his hand a brown tall hat and tan gloves to match. He has his sister’s delicate biscuit complexion, and is built on the same small scale; but he is elastic and strong in muscle, decisive in movement, unexpectedly deeptoned and trenchant in speech, and with perfect manners and a finished personal style which might be envied by a man twice his age. Suavity and self-possession are points of honor with him; and though this, rightly considered, is only the modern mode of boyish self-consciousness, its effect is none the less staggering to his elders, and would be insufferable in a less prepossessing youth. He is promptitude itself, and has a question ready the moment he enters.
Been asking a lot of questions?
As if incapable of doing such a thing.
At the Marine Hotel﻿—half past one.
We shall be able to tell mamma that a respectable Englishman has promised to lunch with us.
Say no more! I haven’t said anything. May I ask whom I have the pleasure of entertaining? It’s really quite impossible for me to lunch at the Marine Hotel with two perfect strangers.
But excuse me: the gentleman I was thinking of is not celebrated.
Well come, Dolly: how do you know you’re not?
But not till we’ve gone, please.
Quite so: we prefer people with unimproved minds. Our own minds are in that fresh and unspoiled condition.
In that case we shall have to introduce him to the other member of the family: the Woman of the Twentieth Century; our sister Gloria!
You were going to improve our minds, I think.
The old story. We talk too much.
He seats himself on the arm of the opposing chair.
She sits down in the writing-table chair, and closes her lips tight with the tips of her fingers.
He looks at them alternately, with emphasis. They meet his gaze like martyrs.
They confirm him by melancholy nods.
He rises with an air of finality, and replaces the stool by the bench.
They go together to the door with perfect dignity.
They halt and turn, arm in arm.
Energetically, throwing off all pretence of a professional manner.
After all, our grandfather is a canon of Lincoln Cathedral.
Like a castaway mariner who sees a sail on the horizon.
It’s too beastly. I won’t stand it any longer, Phil. Here in England everybody asks whether you have a father the very first thing.
I won’t stand it either. Mamma must tell us who he was.
Or who he is. He may be alive.
I hope not. No man alive shall father me.
He might have a lot of money, though.
Two ladies for you, miss. Your mother and sister, miss, I think.
Well, children? How is the toothache, Dolly?
Striking in gravely from the hearth.
Looking round apprehensively at the servant.
The landlord, sir, wishes to speak to you before you go out.
Throwing himself confidentially on her sense of the position.

Not at all, not at all. Your presence here will be the greatest help to me. The fact is, I owe six weeks’ rent; and I’ve had no patients until today. My interview with my landlord will be considerably smoothed by the apparent boom in my business.
Thank you, I’m used to them. Would it be too much to ask you to wait five minutes while I get rid of my landlord downstairs?
He succeeds at last in blundering himself out of the room; but the exhibition is a pitiful one.
Sh﻿—sh, pray, Phil. He may have heard you.
speaking very staccato, with the words detached
Seating herself on the end of the table with a spring.
Indeed? In what way have I given you any reason to complain?
Well, there are certain matters upon which we are beginning to feel that you might take us a little more into your confidence.

Rising, with all the placidity of her age suddenly broken up; and a curious hard excitement, dignified but dogged, ladylike but implacable﻿—the manner of the Old Guard of the Women’s Rights movement﻿—coming upon her.
Touching her shoulder affectionately, soothed even by a gibe from her.
I think it due to ourselves to say that the question we wanted to ask is as much our business as yours.
Besides, it can’t be good to keep a lot of questions bottled up inside you. You did it, mamma; but see how awfully it’s broken out again in me.
I see you want to ask your question. Ask it.
Now look here, Dolly: am I going to conduct this business or are you?

Sh! The result was that the gum architect made considerable difficulties about accepting our invitation to lunch, although I doubt if he has had anything but tea and bread and butter for a fortnight past. Now my knowledge of human nature leads me to believe that we had a father, and that you probably know who he was.
Rising decisively and putting away the stool.
Touching her eyes hastily with her handkerchief and sitting down again.
Do you intend that we shall never know?

She turns away from them and goes up to the easy chair at the fireplace, where she sits down, almost with her back to them. As they wait expectantly, she adds, over her shoulder, with studied indifference.
The answer is pretty obvious. A woman who does not know who her father was cannot accept such an offer.
Surely you did not want to accept it?
Turning a little and raising her voice.
Did that difficulty strike you, Dolly?
But why did you do such a thing, Dolly?
For fun, I suppose. He had to measure my finger for a ring. You’d have done the same thing yourself.
She rises and goes to the hearth.
This is rather a startling departure from Twentieth Century principles.

My dears: I did not say that you were too young to know. I said you were too young to be taken into my confidence. You are very bright children, all of you; but I am glad for your sakes that you are still very inexperienced and consequently very unsympathetic. There are some experiences of mine that I cannot bear to speak of except to those who have gone through what I have gone through. I hope you will never be qualified for such confidences. But I will take care that you shall learn all you want to know. Will that satisfy you?
Leaning forward in her chair and looking earnestly up at her mother.
Meditatively, as if the recollection were a tender one.
I hope I’ve not kept you waiting. That landlord of mine is really an extraordinary old character.
Distracted by her child’s bad manners.
He doesn’t want his rent at all. He’s broken his tooth on a Brazil nut; and he wants me to look at it and to lunch with him afterwards.
Then off with you and bring him up.
Rising and looking at her watch.
The old gentleman with the toothache.
Repeating it to herself like a lesson.
She sits down studiously at the writing-table.
Phil: can you believe such a horrible thing as that about our father﻿—what mother said just now?
Oh, there are lots of people of that kind. Old Chalice used to thrash his wife and daughters with a cartwhip.
He resumes his position on the hearthrug with an elderly and responsible air.
Oh, come! What about your father﻿—the lonely old man with the tender aching heart? He’s pretty well burst up, I think.
Bustling him across to the chair with good-humored peremptoriness.
Gratefully, after looking at her earnestly for a moment.
She feels whether her hat is right.
Well, you have a curious look of my mother.
No, no: nothing. A twinge of memory, Miss Clandon, not of toothache.
Have it out. “Pluck from the memory a rooted sorrow:” with gas, five shillings extra.
His features settle into an implacable frown.
Who has entered the room unobserved, and stolen behind her.
He takes her towards the door.
Taking up his dental mirror and probe from the shelf in front of the cabinet.
He checks himself, and adds, prosaically,
I began using it as a boy because I was made to; and I’ve used it ever since. And I never had toothache in my life.
Don’t you find it rather nasty?

I found that most things that were good for me were nasty. But I was taught to put up with them, and made to put up with them. I’m used to it now: in fact, I like the taste when the soap is really good.
Making a wry face in spite of himself.
He goes to the ledge of cabinet and changes the probe for another one.
It’s not the effect on the teeth: it’s the effect on the character.
He withdraws the probe and again comes to the side of the chair to converse.
Rubbish, man: I want none of your gas. Out with it. People were taught to bear necessary pain in my day.
Oh, if you like being hurt, all right. I’ll hurt you as much as you like, without any extra charge for the beneficial effect on your character.
My good sir: my patients haven’t all formed their characters on kitchen soap.
Suddenly gripping him by the arm as he turns away again to the cabinet.
He nods at him to enforce the effect of this declaration, and releases him.
Oh, come, what do you know about it?
Wincing with a pang of resentment.
He takes the jug from her, and brings it to the cabinet, continuing in the same idle strain.
He stoops to fit the handle on the apparatus by which the chair is raised and lowered.
He grips the arms of the chair and braces himself.
Pausing, with his hand on the lever, to look up at him and say.
Your six weeks’ rent, young man. Don’t you gammon me.
Jumping at the bet and winding him aloft vigorously.
Clutching at the arms of the chair as he falls back.
Deftly stopping him with the gag, and snatching up the mouthpiece of the gas machine.

On the terrace at the Marine Hotel. It is a square flagged platform, with a parapet of heavy oil jar pilasters supporting a broad stone coping on the outer edge, which stands up over the sea like a cliff. The head waiter of the establishment, busy laying napkins on a luncheon table with his back to the sea, has the hotel on his right, and on his left, in the corner nearest the sea, the flight of steps leading down to the beach.

When he looks down the terrace in front of him he sees a little to his left a solitary guest, a middle-aged gentleman sitting on a chair of iron laths at a little iron table with a bowl of lump sugar and three wasps on it, reading the Standard, with his umbrella up to defend him from the sun, which, in August and at less than an hour after noon, is toasting his protended insteps. Just opposite him, at the hotel side of the terrace, there is a garden seat of the ordinary esplanade pattern. Access to the hotel for visitors is by an entrance in the middle of its façade, reached by a couple of steps on a broad square of raised pavement. Nearer the parapet there lurks a way to the kitchen, masked by a little trellis porch. The table at which the waiter is occupied is a long one, set across the terrace with covers and chairs for five, two at each side and one at the end next the hotel. Against the parapet another table is prepared as a buffet to serve from.

The waiter is a remarkable person in his way. A silky old man, white-haired and delicate looking, but so cheerful and contented that in his encouraging presence ambition stands rebuked as vulgarity, and imagination as treason to the abounding sufficiency and interest of the actual. He has a certain expression peculiar to men who have been extraordinarily successful in their calling, and who, whilst aware of the vanity of success, are untouched by envy.

The gentleman at the iron table is not dressed for the seaside. He wears his London frock coat and gloves; and his tall silk hat is on the table beside the sugar bowl. The excellent condition and quality of these garments, the gold-rimmed folding spectacles through which he is reading the Standard, and the Times at his elbow overlaying the local paper, all testify to his respectability. He is about fifty, clean shaven, and close-cropped, with the corners of his mouth turned down purposely, as if he suspected them of wanting to turn up, and was determined not to let them have their way. He has large expansive ears, cod colored eyes, and a brow kept resolutely wide open, as if, again, he had resolved in his youth to be truthful, magnanimous, and incorruptible, but had never succeeded in making that habit of mind automatic and unconscious. Still, he is by no means to be laughed at. There is no sign of stupidity or infirmity of will about him: on the contrary, he would pass anywhere at sight as a man of more than average professional capacity and responsibility. Just at present he is enjoying the weather and the sea too much to be out of patience; but he has exhausted all the news in his papers and is at present reduced to the advertisements, which are not sufficiently succulent to induce him to persevere with them.
Yawning and giving up the paper as a bad job.
Yes, sir. They have a free way with them that is very taking, sir, very taking indeed, sir: especially the young lady and gentleman.
Oh, we must not take what they say too seriously, sir. Of course, sir, if it were true, the young lady would have seen the resemblance, too, sir.
We shall have two more gentlemen at lunch, William.
Peering at her quaintly from under the umbrella.
He shuts the umbrella; puts it aside; and jocularly plants himself with his hands on his hips to be inspected.
She gives him her hand. The shake that ensues is that of old friends after a long separation.
Pointing to the silk hat on the table.
Would you employ a solicitor with a sombrero?
Finch: I see what has happened. You have become respectable.
You hold to your old opinions still?

Howled at! My dear good lady: there is nothing in any of those views nowadays to prevent her from marrying a bishop. You reproached me just now for having become respectable. You were wrong: I hold to our old opinions as strongly as ever. I don’t go to church; and I don’t pretend I do. I call myself what I am: a Philosophic Radical, standing for liberty and the rights of the individual, as I learnt to do from my master Herbert Spencer. Am I howled at? No: I’m indulged as an old fogey. I’m out of everything, because I’ve refused to bow the knee to Socialism.
Yes, Socialism. That’s what Miss Gloria will be up to her ears in before the end of the month if you let her loose here.
No, the theatre. And now to business! Why have you made me come down here?
Well, partly because I wanted to see you﻿—
Her face falling with the most disparagingly obvious disappointment.
Taken aback, but rallying his humor to meet the emergency.
He turns; and she takes his hand and presses it, with a frank straight look into his eyes.
I was christened in a comparatively prosaic mood. My name is﻿—
Completing his sentence for him declamatorily.
Well, so he is: it’s not our fault.
He gives his hand a single shake and drops it; then turns away, exclaiming meditatively,
Have you ordered for seven? Don’t forget the old gentleman.
I have not forgotten him, dear. What is his name?
Changing her tone to a more earnest one.
With a bound, startled and excited.
Oh, Crampstones, or whatever it is. He said I was like his mother. I knew he must mean his daughter.
Because I have seen the gentleman; and he is entirely unfit to be my father, or Dolly’s father, or Gloria’s father, or my mother’s husband.
He has a great deal of money.
I shall not proceed, sir. I am too hurt, too shocked, to proceed.
Which of us is to tell him the truth? Have you thought of that?
Oh, Finch is no good at telling things. Look at the mess he has made of telling us.
I have not been allowed to speak. I protest against this.
Gloria: let us go in. He may arrive at any moment.
Good! Dolly: whose tact were you noticing only this morning?
William: you remember my request to you to regard me as your son?
William: at the very outset of your career as my father, a rival has appeared on the scene.
No, William: this gentleman was very nearly my father: he wooed my mother, but wooed her in vain.
Sh! Consequently, he is only our solicitor. Do you know one Crampton, of this town?
Cockeyed Crampton, sir, of the Crooked Billet, is it?
I don’t know. Finch: does he keep a public house?
We want you to break the news to him, William.
Finch: Your professional incompetence is appalling. William: your sagacity puts us all to shame.
You really are like Shakespeare, William.
Goes back modestly to the luncheon table and lays the two additional covers, one at the end next the steps, and the other so as to make a third on the side furthest from the balustrade.
Seizes his arm and leads him toward the hotel.
Turning for a moment on the steps as she follows them.
He passes his hand over his forehead.
With a sweet smile of welcome.
Helping him to get the overcoat off and taking it from him.

Only his joke, sir, his favourite joke. Yesterday, I was to be his father. Today, as soon as he knew you were coming, sir, he tried to put it up on me that you were his father, his long lost father﻿—not seen you for eighteen years, he said.
Oh, there’s a solicitor with them, is there?
He resumes his study of the menu.
He throws the menu down and goes round the table to look out unconcernedly over the parapet.
He passes on to the table.
He takes the stick and coat into the hotel.
Yes, here﻿—caught in a trap﻿—a mean trap. Are those my children?
He loses countenance himself and stops.
He walks away to the side of the terrace, like a man putting temptation behind him.
Mopping his brow in rage and agony, and yet relieved even by their playing with him.
He utters a half laugh, half sob.
As they all assemble about the table.
She goes to the end of the table nearest the hotel.
Holding the chair for him with inoffensive encouragement.
indicating the side nearest the parapet
Have a six of Irish in it, Finch?
Scowling and about to reply offensively.
You have learnt your lesson from your mother, I see.
Phil: will you please remember that your jokes are apt to irritate people who are not accustomed to us, and that your father is our guest today.
With an obviously forced attempt at cheerful domesticity.
He returns to the service table.
I am keeping my mind open on that subject. William!
How long do you think it would take me to learn to be a really smart waiter?
You don’t happen to have such a thing as a son, yourself, have you?
Is your son a waiter, too, William?
With a touch of melancholy, as if recalling a disappointment softened by time.
He goes into the hotel, leaving the company somewhat overwhelmed by his son’s eminence.
Which of us dare give that man an order again!
I hope he won’t mind my sending him for ginger-beer.
Taken aback, recovers her good humor after a long breath and says sweetly.
Making a fresh effort to lead the conversation into dispassionate regions.
I suppose the Portuguese religion. I never inquired.
The servants come in Lent and kneel down before you and confess all the things they’ve done: and you have to pretend to forgive them. Do they do that in England, William?
Members of the Church of England! What’s the subscription?
Cheese, sir; or would you like a cold sweet?
Bring a box of cigarettes, William.
She rises: they all rise a little.
To take her part against me, you mean.
Intercepting her at the top of the steps and offering her a box of vestas.
Surprised into grateful politeness by the witchery of his sweet and cheerful tones.
Throwing himself back in his chair.
And a bad father? That’s what you mean, eh?
He strikes his fist violently on the table.
They go down the steps together.
He takes up the sunshades again.
For behaving like a bear. What will your daughter think of me for having brought you here?
I was not thinking of what my daughter was thinking of you.
No, you were thinking of yourself. You’re a perfect maniac.
Come, come: they’re only children. The only one of them that’s worth anything called you father.
Taking this in very bad part.
Tackling him very seriously and talking faster and faster.

The explanation is that I’m stark mad, or rather that I’ve never been in my real senses before. I’m capable of anything: I’ve grown up at last: I’m a Man; and it’s your daughter that’s made a man of me.
His words now coming in a perfect torrent.
Not at all, sir, not at all. Very natural, sir, I’m sure, sir, at your age. The lady has sent me for her book, sir. Might I take the liberty of asking you to let her have it at once, sir?
As if the sum were beyond his utmost expectations.
He crosses the terrace to the iron table, and sits down.
Well, I hope he is grateful to you, and recognizes what he owes you.
With another of his irresistible transitions.
He drops a lump of sugar into the tumbler.
I missed that advantage today, I think.
His eyes shining hardly as he props his drawn, miserable face on his hands.
I want to speak with you for a moment.
He rests his head on his hands, and looks down and away from her, in gloomy reflection.

All that is what seems to me so nonsensical, so uncalled for. What do you expect us to feel for you﻿—to do for you? What is it you want? Why are you less civil to us than other people are? You are evidently not very fond of us﻿—why should you be? But surely we can meet without quarrelling.
A dreadful grey shade passing over his face.
Do you know what is due to me as your father?
Rising as if to combat a monster.
Quitting her careless leaning attitude and confronting him promptly and proudly.
She turns away with an evident distaste for that part of the subject, and goes to the luncheon table for a comfortable chair, putting down her book and sunshade.
Turning on him quickly and severely.
She takes one of the luncheon chairs; turns it away from the table; and sits down a little wearily, saying,
Coolly and rationally! No, I can’t. Do you understand that? I can’t.
She frowns, finding such petulance intolerable. He adds hastily,

He stands for a moment, screwing and clinching his brows and hands in his perplexity; then takes the end chair from the luncheon table and sits down beside her, saying, with a touching effort to be gentle and patient,
Then my mother gave me a new name.
You had no right to give me your sister’s name. I don’t know her.
You’re talking nonsense. There are bounds to what I will put up with. I will not have it. Do you hear that?
She looks at him, keeping him in suspense. He forces himself to utter the obnoxious name.
She marks her satisfaction with a slight tightening of the lips, and sits down.
The endearment is so plaintively inept that she smiles in spite of herself, and resigns herself to indulge him a little.
He looks anxiously into her face for some response, and continues less hopefully and more urgently,
He groans involuntarily. She looks at him rather contemptuously and continues,
Stop; or you’ll be sorry afterwards. I’m your father.
How I hate the name! How I love the name of mother! You had better go.
His voice stifles: he is almost in a fit.
Going up to the balustrade with cool, quick resourcefulness, and calling over to the beach.
She returns to the table and pours out a glass of water.
He rises and pulls himself together.
She goes for her book and parasol.
Taken aback for a moment; then answering him with polite but intentional contempt.
She turns away from him with infinite indifference, and sits down with her book on the garden seat.
Instantly changing his tone for one of cordial sincerity, as if he frankly accepted her terms and was delighted and reassured by her principles.
He takes off his hat and throws it gaily on the iron table.
He sits down beside her, so naturally that she does not think of objecting, and proceeds, with enthusiasm,
With a gleam in his eye at the success of his hunter’s guile.
That’s what makes you so inspiring.
Her brow clouds a little. He goes on quickly.
He hesitates, trying to think of a sufficiently unimpassioned word.
As if something were going to happen. It came over me suddenly just before you proposed that we should run away to the others.
She sits down again. He resumes his seat beside her, and watches her with a gravely sympathetic air. She is thoughtful and a little troubled as she adds,
Ah, I wonder! It’s a curiously helpless sensation: isn’t it?

Yes. As if Nature, after allowing us to belong to ourselves and do what we judged right and reasonable for all these years, were suddenly lifting her great hand to take us﻿—her two little children﻿—by the scruffs of our little necks, and use us, in spite of ourselves, for her own purposes, in her own way.
With a new and startling transition to a tone of utter recklessness.
Thrown this enchantment on me. I’m honestly trying to be sensible﻿—scientific﻿—everything that you wish me to be. But﻿—but﻿—oh, don’t you see what you have set to work in my imagination?
With ironical haste to disclaim such a weakness.
He goes to the iron table and takes up his hat.
With elaborate calm, sitting up like a High-school-mistress posing to be photographed.
He pauses and puts his hat down again.
She closes her lips trimly and looks steadily and challengingly at him as she sits more collectedly than ever.
Returning to the end of the garden seat to confront her more emphatically.
Excuse my reminding you that your reason and your knowledge and your experience are not infallible. At least I hope not.
I must believe them. Unless you wish me to believe my eyes, my heart, my instincts, my imagination, which are all telling me the most monstrous lies about you.
He sits down again beside her.
That is ridiculous, and rather personal.
She is ashamed to find that this does not quite please her either.
Beginning to find that she must speak shortly and pointedly to keep her voice steady.
With a stir of feeling beginning to agitate his voice.
And I am a feminine prig.
He turns towards her as if the impulse to touch her were ungovernable: she rises and stands on her guard wrathfully. He springs up impatiently and retreats a step.
Reassured by his withdrawal, and a little remorseful.
Returning to her with all his recklessness of manner replaced by an engaging and chivalrous respect.
She is about to speak: he stops her deprecatingly.
Her principles up in arms at once.
Dropping into the iron chair as if crushed.
He becomes the picture of despair.
Because liking is not enough. Now that I think down into it seriously, I don’t know whether I like you or not.
Looking down at him with wondering concern.
In an agony of restrained passion.
Springing up triumphantly, the agonized voice now solid, ringing, and jubilant.
He seizes her hands: she looks at him in terror.
He draws her to him; kisses her with impetuous strength; and laughs boyishly.
She can only gasp at him.
He runs off buoyantly down the steps.
What is the matter with you?
Blushing unendurably, she covers her face with her hands and turns away from her mother.

The Clandons’ sitting room in the hotel. An expensive apartment on the ground floor, with a French window leading to the gardens. In the centre of the room is a substantial table, surrounded by chairs, and draped with a maroon cloth on which opulently bound hotel and railway guides are displayed. A visitor entering through the window and coming down to this central table would have the fireplace on his left, and a writing table against the wall on his right, next the door, which is further down. He would, if his taste lay that way, admire the wall decoration of Lincrusta Walton in plum color and bronze lacquer, with dado and cornice; the ormolu consoles in the corners; the vases on pillar pedestals of veined marble with bases of polished black wood, one on each side of the window; the ornamental cabinet next the vase on the side nearest the fireplace, its centre compartment closed by an inlaid door, and its corners rounded off with curved panes of glass protecting shelves of cheap blue and white pottery; the bamboo tea table, with folding shelves, in the corresponding space on the other side of the window; the pictures of ocean steamers and Landseer’s dogs; the saddlebag ottoman in line with the door but on the other side of the room; the two comfortable seats of the same pattern on the hearthrug; and finally, on turning round and looking up, the massive brass pole above the window, sustaining a pair of maroon rep curtains with decorated borders of staid green. Altogether, a room well arranged to flatter the occupant’s sense of importance, and reconcile him to a charge of a pound a day for its use.
